extracted.intended_audience: judges, lawyers, forensic examiners, and legal psychologists assessing eyewitness testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for assessing the reliability and limits of human perception (especially sight) in courtroom testimony, with guidance on when to trust, test, or experimentally verify witness statements. Emphasizes individual differences, sensory substitutions, lighting/background effects, and specific phenomena (e.g., retrospective illumination, peripheral color blindness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual variability of sense-perception
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as anything is conceived as passive it may always recur more identically than when it is conceived as active...if Aubert is right then sense-perception is as various as is humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the individuality of perceivers: perceptive power varies with skill, attention, memory, imagination and 'comprehension' method. Do not assume two different descriptions of the same event imply falsehood — they may reflect different perceptual composition. Compare observers and consider personality/skill differences before judging accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional (compounding) nature of visual apperception
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual perception compounds a group of the smallest conditions into what we take as an instantaneous impression; different observers may compound elements (a,b,c,d...) in different groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect large differences in reports because observers unconsciously group visual elements differently (e.g., dyads, triads). Use this to explain divergent descriptions rather than immediately concluding deceit or inattention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed of apperception affects reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The speed of apperception has been subjected to measurement...results show 0.015 to 0.035 seconds for compounded images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that rapid events may not be fully apprehended; witnesses may only perceive compounded images. Where timing of perception matters, note apperception speed differences (clever vs slow observers) and, if possible, obtain comparative measures or corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicariousness/substitution of the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: There is that so-called vicariousness of the senses which substitutes one sense for another, in representation...some person heard without seeing him, will imagine a definite face which are pure imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask urgent, specific questions to determine whether a witness actually saw something or merely heard/smelled/imagined it. Be aware that sensitive or imaginative persons are particularly prone to substituting senses (e.g., thinking they saw someone they only heard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective illumination of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrospective illumination consists in the appearance of a sense-perception under conditions of some noticeable interruption...the latent stimulus caused by the ticking worked backward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a witness may become consciously aware of earlier stimuli only after a later disturbance (e.g., a scream), and thus 'see' events only retrospectively. In sudden events determine what was actually perceived versus what became conscious later; this is especially important in criminal trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat visual testimony as inherently indubitable
rubrics_metrics.description: If we compare sight with the hearing...we discover the well-known fact that what is seen is much more certain and trustworthy than what is heard...but ... people know little of optical illusions and false visual perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although people commonly trust visual testimony, judges should be aware of numerous optical illusions and perceptual errors. Cross-check visual claims with other senses, physical experiments, or corroboration rather than assuming visual truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation-driven interpolation (perceptual bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: We interpolate objects in the lacunæ of vision according to our expectations...When ten people in an inn see how A raises a beer glass...five expect 'Now he'll pound him,' and five others: 'Now he'll throw it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for expectation-based interpretations: identical visual input may be reported differently depending on observers' anticipations. Before accusing witnesses of lying, consider perceptual bias from expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective and anthropocentric vision affecting size/distance judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Liebmann: 'we see things only in perspective sizes...we know only relations of magnitude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When witnesses testify about size or distance, ask whence they observed it and, where feasible, experimentally verify (e.g., recreate viewing angles). Be cautious about trusting untested size/distance estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illumination and background strongly influence visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctness of objects depends upon absolute brightness and differences in brightness...the intensity of the object with regard to its background has yet to be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims about visibility under certain lighting, conduct experiments under the same conditions (judge or third party). Determine both object color/brightness and background before accepting claims about what could be seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences in far/near-sightedness and adaptation to darkness
rubrics_metrics.description: The human eye is so very different in each man...before an assertion of a short-sighted man is doubted an experiment should be made, or at least another trustworthy short-sighted person should be asked...The longer you are in darkness the more you see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish witness' visual acuity and acclimatization (e.g., long-term dark adaptation). If a short- or long-sighted person's claim is at issue, verify by experiment or consult another similar-vision person before discounting testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long thin objects remain visible at much greater distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthy objects like poles, wires, etc., are visible at incomparably greater distances than, e.g., squares of the same length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account object shape when evaluating distance visibility claims (telephone wires/long thin objects may be seen at surprising ranges). Do not dismiss claims of seeing thin objects at distance without considering this phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixation difficulty and disappearance of small points
rubrics_metrics.description: A point seen for a considerable time may easily disappear from perception...If we fix a distant point it is disappearing at every instant...if however we fix upon a long, thin body...we may see the object with a wandering eye, hence more clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to explain sudden disappearance reports (esp. at night). When witnesses report objects 'vanishing', consider peripheral/fixation effects rather than deliberate falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moonlight and low-light overestimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-estimation of the moon's illuminating power...the power of the full moon is not more than that of a candle twelve feet away...an intimate may be recognized at from fifteen to sixteen meters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of clear recognition by moonlight skeptically; use standard measures (e.g., known recognition distances by moon phase) or recreate conditions to test visibility claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innervation/motor mimicry from seeing movement can be misread as complicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The sight of a man carrying a heavy load made him feel tension in the muscles involved...In many cases suspects were accused of complicity simply because they were making suspicious movements...the suspects were harmless spectators who were simply more obvious in their innervation of the muscles involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that visual stimuli can elicit involuntary muscular responses that may appear suspicious. Do not infer intent or complicity solely from observed preparatory or tense movements; investigate whether movements could be automatic innervation from witnessing the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binocular vision rarely crucial but note one-eye observations
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not believe that binocular vision is of much importance in the law...a part of what we see is seen with one eye only...This may be of importance when an effect has been observed first with both eyes, then with one;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally binocular vs monocular vision is not decisive, but ask whether witness viewed with one or both eyes when relevant (e.g., sudden occlusion or objects presented close to face), as it can affect which parts of a scene were actually seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color vision: determine normality and gaze when color matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When the question of color is raised, therefore, we will try to discover only whether the person in question has normal color-vision...the retina will not see red at the periphery...If, then, a witness has not looked right at a definitely red object, and has seen it askance, he has certainly not observed its color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test witnesses for color-normal vision when color identification is material. If color claims depend on peripheral viewing, be skeptical—red is not perceived at periphery. Use simple experiments to check gaze direction and color perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color recognizability depends on background and angular size (Aubert data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aubert constructed double squares...determined the angle of vision at which the color as such could be seen (table of angles for colors on white/black backgrounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When color identification at distance is asserted, establish both the color and the background (white vs black) and consider the required angular size; where possible, replicate conditions or consult measured thresholds (e.g., Aubert's angles) to test plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of color disappearance in dimming may inform testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: It is well known that in the diminution of brightnesses red disappears before blue...So if anybody asserts that he has been able to see the blue of a man's coat but not his red-brown trousers, his statement is possibly true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge about relative persistence of colors in low light (some colors disappear before others) to assess claims about seeing particular colors at twilight or dusk; though orders reported are not fully consistent, this principle can help evaluate plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color and contour affect perceived size
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantz: objects in less refractable colors (red, orange, yellow, and purple) look 0.2 to 3.6% bigger against white...blue...appear smaller. Dark and long-lined objects seem longer; bright and horizontal seem wider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that color and object shape bias size judgments. When size is material, consider these perceptual distortions and, if necessary, obtain experimental verification or corroborative measurements.
